overview: This two-page State Department “List of Papers” inventories correspondence filed under calamities in Japanese-ruled Taiwan, chiefly the destructive earthquake of April 21, 1935. The indexed papers report casualties and damage in Hsinchu and Taichung, confirm the safety of Americans, record exchanges of condolence among American and Japanese leaders, and document proposals and discussions concerning American Red Cross, naval, and other relief assistance. Later entries concern official damage estimates, another earthquake in Hsinchu Province that killed 49 people, and a typhoon that struck Taiwan on August 30, 1940; the underlying telegrams and letters themselves are not reproduced here.

subfiles.about: A two-page index summarizes correspondence concerning earthquakes and relief efforts in Taiwan during 1935 and a typhoon there in 1940.
subfiles.summary: The list begins with reports of the April 21, 1935 earthquake in Hsinchu and Taichung and assurances that known Americans were unharmed. It inventories presidential, imperial, and foreign-ministry messages of condolence, private appeals for assistance, and exchanges between the American and Japanese Red Cross societies over whether outside relief was needed. Subsequent entries cite official damage estimates, a later Hsinchu Province earthquake causing 49 deaths and 134 injuries, and a report on the August 30, 1940 Taiwan typhoon. The list provides document numbers, dates, correspondents, routing information, and short descriptions, but not the full texts of the indexed papers.

interest: The index is useful for reconstructing a diplomatic and humanitarian correspondence chain even though the underlying papers are absent. It shows both spontaneous American proposals—ranging from tents and supplies in Manila to dispatching the naval fleet—and the Japanese Red Cross response that domestic arrangements were sufficient. It also documents the rapid verification of American safety, formal exchanges between Roosevelt and Hirohito, and later official casualty and damage reporting, offering a compact view of how the State Department managed disaster information and relief diplomacy in colonial Taiwan.
